questions.q: In Chart.yaml, why are `version` and `appVersion` tracked as two separate fields?
options: They are not actually separate — Helm treats them as aliases of the same value
`version` tracks the chart's own templates/structure; `appVersion` tracks the version of the application the chart deploys, and they change independently
`appVersion` is deprecated and ignored by Helm 3
`version` must always match the Kubernetes API version
questions.explain: The chart (its templates and structure) and the application it deploys evolve on different timelines — a new product-catalog image can ship (appVersion changes) with zero changes to the chart's templates (version stays the same), and vice versa.

questions.q: In templates/deployment.yaml, what does `{{ .Release.Name }}` resolve to?
options: The chart's name as written in Chart.yaml, always
A random string generated by Helm on every install
The name given to `helm install <name> ...` for this specific release
The current Kubernetes namespace
questions.explain: .Release.Name is a built-in object set to whatever release name was passed to helm install, which is how the same template can produce distinctly named resources for different releases of the same chart.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between `helm lint` and `helm template`?
options: They are identical commands with different names
helm lint installs a test release; helm template only checks syntax
helm lint checks the chart's structure and syntax without rendering output; helm template actually renders the final YAML Helm would apply, without touching the cluster
helm template requires a live cluster connection; helm lint does not
questions.explain: helm lint is a structural/syntax check. helm template goes further and produces the literal rendered manifests, letting you read the exact YAML before anything is applied — neither one touches a cluster.

questions.q: A values.yaml sets `resources.requests.cpu: "250m"`. In the Deployment template, which expression correctly inserts the whole resources block as YAML, properly indented under a container spec?
options: resources: {{ .Values.resources }}
resources:\n  {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
resources: "{{ .Values.resources.requests.cpu }}"
Templates cannot insert nested YAML blocks like this
questions.explain: toYaml converts a nested values structure into YAML text, and nindent reindents it to the correct level inside the surrounding manifest — the standard pattern for inserting blocks like resources or nodeSelector from values.yaml.

questions.q: Why run `helm template` before `helm install` or `helm upgrade` in a real workflow?
options: It is required by Kubernetes before any chart can be installed
It lets you read the exact rendered YAML locally and catch a template syntax or logic error before it reaches the cluster
It automatically fixes any errors found in the chart
It uploads the chart to a Helm repository
questions.explain: helm template renders with no cluster interaction, so reviewing its output is the cheapest way to catch a broken {{ }} expression or missing value before an install or upgrade actually changes anything running.
